ta-l1d43q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 43. Lombard excludes the error of those who limited God's power, saying it is not simply of all things: first as they limited it to the things that are made, then (Dist. 44) as they limited it to their quality, saying God cannot make other or better things than he makes. He reports their position, their plausible arguments, invented causes, and authorities, answering them, and adduces authorities for the truth: God can do many things he does not will and can leave undone what he does. Since they held that God cannot do anything he does not do, denying the infinity of divine power, and that he cannot not do what he does, implying necessity, Thomas asks two questions: on the infinity of divine power and on whether God acts by necessity. On the first, whether God's power is infinite, and whether omnipotence is communicable to a creature.
claims: God can do more than he does and can leave undone what he does.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e124.summary: First argument that God's power is not infinite. The infinite has the character of part and matter, so of the imperfect (the Philosopher), and God's power is most perfect.
claims: The infinite is imperfect.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e127.summary: Second argument. Finite and infinite belong to quantity (the Philosopher), and every quantity is divisible, but divine power is simple.
claims: Infinity belongs to quantity.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e130.summary: Third argument. An active power with no corresponding passive power in nature would be in vain (philosophers), and no passive power can receive an infinite effect.
claims: Active power needs a proportioned passive power.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e134.summary: Fourth argument. Nothing infinite can be comprehended, since what is comprehended has its limits surveyed (Augustine), and the divine intellect comprehends its power.
claims: God comprehends his power.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e137.summary: Fifth argument. Every power can be actualized, so an infinite power could make infinitely many things in act, and then either it could make more, so something would exceed the infinite, or not, so it would be exhausted and finite.
claims: An actualized infinite power is contradictory.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e140.summary: Sed contra. In infinite magnitude there is infinite power (philosophers), whether magnitude of bulk, impossible to be infinite, or of power, and Ps. 144:3 says of his greatness there is no end.
claims: His greatness has no end.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e146.summary: Thomas's determination. The infinite is taken privatively, which does not fit God, since nothing is said of him privatively (Dist. 7), or negatively, and so God is infinite as in no way limited (Damascene). Some, taking finite and infinite only as properties of quantity, found infinity in God only as virtual quantity, saying he is infinite because his power is, and so some denied that God's essence as essence is infinite and claimed the saints see it, which is erroneous. Rather, 'end' or 'term' is said in many ways (the Philosopher): the term of quantity, as a point of a line, from whose position or privation finite and infinite are properties of quantity, not in incorporeals; and the end of essence, as the last constitutive difference terminates a species' essence, so what signifies essence is called definition or term, and each thing is limited by what determines or contracts its essence: a genus, of itself indifferent to many, by one difference; prime matter, indifferent to all forms and so called infinite, by form; and form, which of itself can perfect various parts of matter, by the matter receiving it. From the negation of this end the divine essence is called infinite. Every form considered abstractly has infinity in its own concept, as whiteness abstractly understood is not limited, though the concepts of colour and being are determined and contracted in it to a species. So what has absolute being, not received in anything, but is its own being, is infinite simply, and so his essence, goodness, and all else said of him are infinite, since none is limited as what is received is limited to the recipient's capacity. From the infinity of essence follows infinity of power, as the Liber de causis says the first being has simply infinite power because it is its own power.
claims: God's essence is infinite negatively, since his being is unreceived and so unlimited.
His infinite power follows from his infinite essence, not conversely.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e149.summary: Reply to the first argument. The objection concerns the privatively infinite, what is apt to have an end and lacks it, whose character consists in matter with privation, which does not fit God.
claims: The imperfect infinite is privative.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e152.summary: Reply to the second argument. The objection concerns the infinite as privation of the term of quantity.
claims: Quantitative infinity is not divine infinity.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e156.summary: Reply to the third argument. God's active power is not for an end but is the end of all, so though no passive power equals it, it is not in vain, since 'in vain' is what is for an end it does not reach; other active and passive powers approach it as far as they can.
claims: Divine power is the end of all, not in vain.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e159.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Comprehension includes two things: grasping or containing a thing's limits, and so the infinite is in no way comprehended, by finite or infinite, nor does God comprehend himself thus, having no limits; and nothing of the comprehended being outside the comprehender, and so the divine intellect comprehends its essence and power, since nothing is outside it.
claims: God comprehends himself as nothing escapes him, not by grasping limits.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e162.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. No effect is produced by a power in a way contrary to its concept, as a motive power does not make all parts of motion simultaneous, which would no longer be motion; such an act is infinite (Physics 3), always mixed with potency, actualized only successively. So it does not follow that God can make actual all the infinite things he can, since then the infinite would be finite.
claims: Divine power cannot actualize an infinite whole, which would contradict infinity.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e174.summary: First argument that God's omnipotence can be communicated to a creature. His omnipotence is not nobler than his goodness, which is communicated to creatures.
claims: Goodness is communicated.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e177.summary: Second argument. Having all knowledge belongs to divine perfection as having all power does, and knowledge extends further, to good and evil, and knowledge of all was communicated to Christ's soul.
claims: Christ's soul knows all.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e180.summary: Third argument. Faith makes all things possible ('nothing is impossible to the believer', Matt. 17), and faith is infused in creatures.
claims: Nothing is impossible to faith.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e184.summary: Fourth argument. Every power separate from matter is infinite (philosophers), since no proportion holds between material and separate power, and angels are separate substances (Dionysius), and God is omnipotent by the infinity of his power.
claims: Separate powers are infinite.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e187.summary: Sed contra. The creation of each thing belongs to God's power, and no thing can be given to confer being on itself by creating.
claims: No creature can create itself.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e190.summary: Second sed contra. Whatever divine perfection is communicable to a creature was communicated to Christ's soul, and omnipotence was not (Book III).
claims: Christ's soul lacks omnipotence.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e193.summary: Thomas's determination. Power always follows essence, so a finite essence cannot have infinite power, and no created essence can be infinite, since its being is not absolute and subsistent but received in something; if it were absolute being it would not differ from divine being, since there can be no plurality of a nature, like whiteness or life, except as one is absolute and another joined to something, or both received in different things, since each thing's substance is all at once (Metaphysics 5). So as it cannot be communicated to a creature to be God, neither to have infinite essence, infinite power, or omnipotence.
claims: Omnipotence cannot be communicated, since power follows essence and no created essence is infinite.
Absolute, unreceived being cannot be multiplied.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e196.summary: Reply to the first argument. Every perfection in creatures is modelled on divine perfection but is more perfect in God and cannot be in creatures in his mode, so every name designating a divine perfection absolutely, without connoting a mode, is communicable to creatures (power, wisdom, goodness), but every name connoting the mode in which it is in God is incommunicable (being the supreme good, omnipotent).
claims: Perfections are communicable; their divine mode is not.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e199.summary: Reply to the second argument. Power is signified as going out from the essence, so infinite power cannot be communicated to a finite essence, but the soul's knowledge is by receiving, so by union with something infinite as object it can have all knowledge, and so Christ's soul sees all in the Word.
claims: Knowledge receives, so it can extend to all; power issues from essence, so it cannot.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the third argument. The distribution is accommodated: faith's power extends not to all things absolutely, like creating the heavens, but to what confirms faith, raising the dead and healing the sick, and these are done not by a created power in the believer but by uncreated power at the believer's prayer, so man does them neither per se nor a se; they are attributed to faith because what is believed is in a way proved by miracles (Mark 16:20).
claims: Miracles of faith are done by God's power at the believer's prayer.

ta-l1d43q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. There and in the Liber de causis the power of a created intelligence is said not to be simply infinite, since it is not subsistent but received in a subsistent, and no intelligence is its own power. It is called infinite downward, not upward: compared to God it is finite, receiving divine power not in its whole infinity but in its own mode; compared to what is below it, infinite, as able to move infinitely and produce infinitely many effects by motion, on the philosophers' view that intelligences move the orbs, as the sun's power can be called infinite downward, since infinitely many things could be generated by it if the world lasted forever.
claims: Angelic power is infinite only downward, finite upward.

ta-l1d43q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 43 divides Lombard's refutation of those who limited God's power to what he does and to its present quality, and announces two questions, on the infinity of divine power and on necessity in God's action.
claims: God can do more than he does.

ta-l1d43q1-Dd1e116.summary: Article 1 holds that God's essence is infinite negatively, since his being is unreceived and so unlimited by any recipient, and that his infinite power follows from it. Privative and quantitative infinity do not apply. His power is the end of all, not in vain. He comprehends himself as nothing escapes him, not by grasping limits, and his power cannot actualize an infinite whole.
claims: God's infinite power follows from his infinite, unreceived being.

ta-l1d43q1-Dd1e166.summary: Article 2 holds that omnipotence cannot be communicated to a creature, since power follows essence and no created essence can be infinite. Perfections are communicable but not their divine mode. Christ's soul knows all by receiving but is not omnipotent, faith's miracles are by God's power, and angelic power is infinite only downward.
claims: Omnipotence is incommunicable to creatures.

ta-l1d43q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 43 treats the infinity of divine power. Article 1 holds that God's essence is infinite negatively, his being unreceived and unlimited, and that his power is infinite as following from it. Article 2 holds that omnipotence cannot be communicated to any creature, since power follows essence and every created essence is finite, received being.
claims: God's power is infinite because his being is unreceived.
Omnipotence is incommunicable.
